newsitem.title: UK: Blair to continue UK revolution with legislation.
newsitem.headline: Blair to continue UK revolution with legislation.

text.p: Prime Minister Tony Blair on Tuesday put the finishing touches to a crowded initial legislative programme that aides said would start to fulfil the core policy promises that swept his Labour party to power.
Blair, who has hit the ground running since he won a landslide election victory on May 1, is proposing to push 26 bills through parliament over the next 17 months.
A senior official said the main theme was to equip Britain for the future and unify the country after what he called 18 years of dogma and division under the vanquished Conservatives.
Blair will tell parliament on Wednesday that he ran for office as "New Labour" on a one-nation platform aimed at healing social divisions and that was how he intended to govern.
"We are the people's government," Blair intends to say, according to an aide. "People feel they have a government back, a government determined to serve them."

Officials said the core of the programme was directed at implementing Labour's five core manifesto pledges -- to cut primary school class sizes, shorten hospital waiting listss, crack down on young thugs, get 250,000 young people off welfare into work and to create the conditions for lasting prosperity.
Two education bills form the centrepiece of the legislative programme, constititing what Blair believes is the "most fundamental attack on under-achievement since the war".

The programme, which will be read out on Wednesday by head-of-state Queen Elizabeth in a glittering centuries-old ceremony in the upper House of Lords, will also include some of the most radical constitutional reforms in Britain for decades.

Blair intends to harness his commanding 179 majority in the 659-seat House of Commons to set up mini-parliaments for Scotland and Wales and to bring in Britain's first law protecting personal privacy, which may also address widespread concern about media intrusion.

Blair's deputy, John Prescott, said the programme would underline the new government's commitment to change and finally silence those who criticised the party during the campaign as being indistinguishable from the ousted Conservatives.

"You can see and feel the commitment to change which marks this government -- just look what we have achieved in only the first 10 days. We have started sweeping away the cobwebs left over Whitehall by the last government," Prescott said.
In a pep talk to new Labour members of parliament, Prescott said the programme would maintain the momentum and mark the first steps to another election victory in five years' time.
"In just 10 days we have shown that this Labour government will be dynamic and radical, not just for five years but, with the support of the electorate, for 10 years at least," he said.

The first Labour government to be elected since 1974 has galvanised politics and policy-making since it took office, transferring ministerial power over interest rates to the Bank of England and embarking on a charm offensive to repair Britain's frayed relations with Europe.
One bill to be trailed on Wednesday would scrap some of the Conservatives' controversial market-oriented health reforms.

Another would ban all handguns in response to last year's murder of 16 infants and their teacher at a Scottish school. The Conservatives had permitted handguns with a calibre lower than .22, saying they were used mainly for sporting competitions.
